subject: biology
topicDisplay: A1–A2 — Unity and diversity: molecules and cells
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Life happens in water: cells are aqueous, wherever they live
Polar bonds inside the molecule; hydrogen bonds between molecules
Cohesion: water sticks to water
Water is the solvent for metabolism and transport
Water's physical properties shape life in it
DNA is the genetic material of every living organism
A nucleotide has three parts, with the sugar in the middle
Four bases in each nucleic acid form the code
RNA is a polymer built by condensation of nucleotides
How DNA and RNA differ: strands, sugar, bases
Complementary pairing lets DNA be copied and expressed
Any length, any sequence: DNA's storage capacity has no limit
One genetic code for all life points to one common ancestor
Using a light microscope and calculating size
Newer microscopy techniques and what each one gains
Prokaryotic cell structure
One cell can carry out every function of life
How animal, fungal and plant cells differ
Recognizing cell types and organelles in micrographs
Drawing and annotating cell structures from micrographs

questions.q: Water is described as the medium for life. What does this mean?
options: Most of the processes of life take place in aqueous solution.
Water is inert packing between the working parts of a cell.
Every substance that a cell uses must be dissolved in water.
Life processes occur in water only in aquatic organisms.
optionWhy: The first cells originated in water, and water remains the medium in which most processes of life occur: metabolic reactions happen in the aqueous cytoplasm and substances are transported dissolved in water.
A student who sees water as passive packaging picks this. Water is not filler between the active parts: the aqueous cytoplasm is where most of the cell's reactions actually occur.
A student who thinks nothing useful can be insoluble picks this. Some molecules, such as the hydrophobic tails of membrane phospholipids, function precisely because they do not dissolve.
A student who confuses habitat with medium picks this. Land and flying organisms carry water inside their cells, and their metabolism still takes place in aqueous solution.
questions.explain: The first cells originated in water, and water remains the medium in which most processes of life occur: metabolic reactions happen in the aqueous cytoplasm and substances are transported dissolved in water.

questions.q: Why is each covalent bond between oxygen and hydrogen in a water molecule polar?
options: Each hydrogen atom gives up its electron completely to the oxygen atom.
The shared electrons are drawn more strongly towards the oxygen atom.
It is a hydrogen bond, and hydrogen bonds are polar by their nature.
Oxygen and hydrogen atoms behave as opposite magnetic poles.
optionWhy: A student who treats the δ charges as full ionic charges picks this. In a polar covalent bond the electrons are shared unequally, not transferred; no ions form.

Oxygen attracts the shared electron pair more strongly than hydrogen does, so the electrons are shared unequally: oxygen becomes δ− and each hydrogen δ+. This unequal sharing is what makes the bond polar.
A student who thinks the bond inside the molecule is a hydrogen bond picks this. The O–H bond is a polar covalent bond; hydrogen bonds form between molecules because of that polarity.
A student who reads 'polar' as magnetic picks this. Polarity here is an uneven distribution of electric charge caused by unequal sharing of electrons, not magnetism.
questions.explain: Oxygen attracts the shared electron pair more strongly than hydrogen does, so the electrons are shared unequally: oxygen becomes δ− and each hydrogen δ+. This unequal sharing is what makes the bond polar.

questions.q: Transpiration puts the column of water in a xylem vessel under tension. Why does the column not break as it is pulled upwards?
options: Root pressure pushes the column upwards from below.
Capillary action lifts the water inside the narrow vessel.
Hydrogen bonds within each molecule resist the pull.
Hydrogen bonds hold the molecules to each other.
optionWhy: A student who thinks water is pushed up from the roots picks this. The column in a transpiring plant is pulled from above and is under tension; what stops it breaking is the attraction between the water molecules.
A student who thinks capillary rise carries water up the whole plant picks this. Capillary action moves water only short distances; the column is held together under tension by cohesion.

A student who locates hydrogen bonds inside the water molecule picks this. The bonds within a molecule are polar covalent bonds; the hydrogen bonds that keep the column continuous are between neighbouring molecules.

Cohesion due to hydrogen bonding keeps the water molecules attached to one another, so the tension created by evaporation in the leaves is transmitted down the whole column and water is drawn up without the column separating.
questions.explain: Cohesion due to hydrogen bonding keeps the water molecules attached to one another, so the tension created by evaporation in the leaves is transmitted down the whole column and water is drawn up without the column separating.

questions.q: Why do so many different substances dissolve in water?
options: Water splits every solute into positive and negative ions.
Water breaks the covalent bonds within the solute molecules.
Water molecules are magnetic and so attract other substances.
Polar water molecules attract polar and charged solutes.
optionWhy: A student who thinks dissolving always means forming ions picks this. Ionic compounds do separate into ions, but polar molecules such as glucose dissolve intact by hydrogen bonding to water.
A student who thinks dissolving is a chemical breakdown picks this. Dissolving is a physical change: the solute's molecules stay whole and become surrounded by water molecules.
A student who reads 'polar' as magnetic picks this. Water's polarity is an uneven distribution of electric charge, and it attracts solutes electrically, not magnetically.

The δ+ and δ− regions of water molecules are attracted to charged particles and to the polar groups of molecules, so a wide variety of hydrophilic substances dissolve. This is why water is the medium for metabolism and transport.
questions.explain: The δ+ and δ− regions of water molecules are attracted to charged particles and to the polar groups of molecules, so a wide variety of hydrophilic substances dissolve. This is why water is the medium for metabolism and transport.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes a consequence of the physical properties of water for a ringed seal (Pusa hispida)?
options: Because it can sink, the water gives its body no support.
It loses heat slowly because water is a poor conductor of heat.
Upthrust from the sea water supports most of its body weight.
The sea stays warm because of water's high specific heat capacity.
optionWhy: A student who thinks upthrust acts only on floating objects picks this. Upthrust acts on any immersed body; the seal's density is close to that of water, so most of its weight is supported.
A student who merges specific heat capacity with conductivity picks this. Water conducts heat about 25 times faster than air, so the seal loses heat rapidly and needs thick blubber.
Water is dense, so the upthrust on the seal's body is close to its weight (buoyancy). The seal needs far less skeletal support than a land animal, which receives negligible upthrust from air.
A student who reads 'high heat capacity' as 'warm' picks this. High specific heat capacity makes the sea's temperature stable, not warm; Arctic sea water is close to 0 °C.
questions.explain: Water is dense, so the upthrust on the seal's body is close to its weight (buoyancy). The seal needs far less skeletal support than a land animal, which receives negligible upthrust from air.

questions.q: Which statement about the genetic material of organisms is correct?
options: Every living organism, from bacteria to humans, uses DNA as its genetic material.
Some living organisms use RNA in place of DNA as their genetic material.
Genetic information in cells is stored in proteins rather than in DNA.
Living organisms vary in whether their genes are made of DNA or RNA.
optionWhy: DNA is the genetic material of all living organisms. The only entities that use RNA as genetic material are certain viruses, and viruses are not considered to be living.
A student who counts RNA viruses as living organisms picks this. Viruses are not considered to be living, so no living organism uses RNA as its genetic material.
A student who confuses a gene with its protein product picks this. Genes are lengths of DNA; the protein is what the gene's base sequence specifies, not the store of information.
A student who has generalized from RNA viruses picks this. Every living organism uses DNA; RNA viruses do not count because viruses are not living.
questions.explain: DNA is the genetic material of all living organisms. The only entities that use RNA as genetic material are certain viruses, and viruses are not considered to be living.

questions.q: Which is a correct description of a single nucleotide?
options: A nitrogenous base only; the sugar and phosphate belong to the backbone.
A phosphate group bonded to a nitrogenous base, which is bonded to a sugar.
A pentose sugar bonded to a phosphate group and to a nitrogenous base.
A six-carbon sugar, glucose, bonded to a phosphate and to a base.
optionWhy: A student who uses 'base' and 'nucleotide' as synonyms picks this. The sugar and phosphate that make up the backbone are parts of each nucleotide, along with its base.
A student who reads the circle–pentagon–rectangle diagram as a chain picks this. The phosphate and the base are each bonded to the sugar; they are not bonded to each other.
A nucleotide has three components: a pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base. The sugar is central, with the phosphate and the base each bonded to it.
A student who takes 'sugar' to mean glucose picks this. The sugar of a nucleotide is a pentose, with five carbon atoms: ribose or deoxyribose.
questions.explain: A nucleotide has three components: a pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base. The sugar is central, with the phosphate and the base each bonded to it.

questions.q: Which list names the nitrogenous bases found in DNA?
options: Adenine, cytosine, guanine and uracil: four bases.
Adenine, cytosine, guanine and thymine: four bases.
Adenine, cytosine, guanine, thymine and uracil.
Alanine, cysteine, glycine and threonine: four bases.
optionWhy: A student who attaches uracil to the wrong nucleic acid picks this. Uracil is found in RNA, where it takes the place of thymine; DNA contains thymine.
DNA contains four bases: adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) and thymine (T). The order of these bases along the strand forms the basis of the genetic code.
A student who has pooled every base name into one list picks this. Each nucleic acid has exactly four bases; uracil is not found in DNA.

A student who blurs DNA with protein picks this: alanine, cysteine, glycine and threonine are amino acids, the monomers of protein, whose names resemble the DNA bases adenine, cytosine, guanine and thymine. The bases of DNA are adenine, cytosine, guanine and thymine.
questions.explain: DNA contains four bases: adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) and thymine (T). The order of these bases along the strand forms the basis of the genetic code.

questions.q: How is a molecule of RNA formed from nucleotides?
options: Hydrolysis reactions join nucleotides through their sugars and phosphates, taking in a water molecule each time.
Hydrogen bonds form between the phosphate group of one nucleotide and the sugar of the next in the chain.
Condensation reactions bond the phosphate of one nucleotide to the sugar of the next, releasing water.
Condensation reactions bond the base of one nucleotide to the base of the next, releasing water.
optionWhy: A student who has condensation and hydrolysis the wrong way round picks this. Hydrolysis breaks polymers by adding water; nucleotides are joined by condensation, which releases water.
A student who thinks hydrogen bonds are the bonds of nucleic acids picks this. The bonds linking nucleotides in a strand are covalent, formed by condensation.
RNA is a polymer formed by condensation of nucleotide monomers. Each condensation forms a covalent sugar–phosphate bond and releases one molecule of water.
A student who pictures the bases as the links in the chain picks this. Condensation occurs between the phosphate of one nucleotide and the sugar of the next; the bases are not joined to each other.
questions.explain: RNA is a polymer formed by condensation of nucleotide monomers. Each condensation forms a covalent sugar–phosphate bond and releases one molecule of water.

questions.q: Which row correctly gives differences between DNA and RNA?
options: DNA: two strands, deoxyribose, thymine. RNA: one strand, deoxyribose, thymine.
DNA: two strands, ribose, thymine. RNA: one strand, deoxyribose, uracil.
DNA: two strands, deoxyribose, thymine. RNA: one strand, ribose and uracil.
DNA: two strands, deoxyribose, thymine. RNA: two strands, ribose, uracil.
optionWhy: A student who thinks RNA is simply one strand of DNA picks this. RNA also differs in its sugar (ribose) and in having uracil instead of thymine.
A student who has the sugars the wrong way round picks this. Deoxyribose (one oxygen fewer than ribose) is the sugar of DNA, as its name says; ribose is the sugar of RNA.
DNA is double-stranded, contains the pentose deoxyribose and has thymine; RNA is single-stranded, contains ribose and has uracil in place of thymine.
A student who draws every nucleic acid as a double helix picks this. RNA is single-stranded; the number of strands is one of the three differences between the molecules.
questions.explain: DNA is double-stranded, contains the pentose deoxyribose and has thymine; RNA is single-stranded, contains ribose and has uracil in place of thymine.

questions.q: How does complementary base pairing allow the genetic information in a DNA molecule to be replicated?
options: Each separated strand is a template on which free nucleotides pair by hydrogen bonding, so both new molecules keep the original sequence.
Each separated strand acts as a template on which free nucleotides pair by covalent bonding, so both new molecules carry the original sequence.
Each strand is copied directly, base for base, so the new strand is identical to the strand it was built against, preserving the sequence.
Only one strand acts as a template, because the other strand has the same base sequence and would give exactly the same product if it were copied too.
optionWhy: Because each base can hydrogen-bond stably only with its complement, the sequence of a template strand determines the sequence of the strand built against it. Both strands serve as templates, so two identical molecules result.
A student who assumes the pairing is covalent picks this. Complementarity is based on hydrogen bonding; the covalent bonds formed during replication are those of the new backbone.
A student who thinks copying means making an identical strand picks this. The new strand is complementary to its template; the original sequence is restored only across the pair of strands.
A student who thinks the two strands are identical picks this. The strands are complementary, and both act as templates so that each daughter molecule has one old and one new strand.
questions.explain: Because each base can hydrogen-bond stably only with its complement, the sequence of a template strand determines the sequence of the strand built against it. Both strands serve as templates, so two identical molecules result.

questions.q: How many different base sequences are possible for a single DNA strand that is 10 nucleotides long?
options: 4 × 10, which is exactly 40
10⁴, which is exactly 10 000
4¹⁰, which is about 1 000 000
2¹⁰, which is exactly 1024
optionWhy: A student who combines the two numbers by multiplying them picks this. The possibilities multiply at each position, giving 4¹⁰, not 4 × 10.
A student who puts the numbers into the wrong places in the power picks this. It is the number of bases (4) raised to the number of positions (10): 4¹⁰.
Each of the 10 positions can be any of four bases, independently of the others, so the number of possible sequences is 4 × 4 × … (10 times) = 4¹⁰ = 1 048 576.
A student who counts two kinds of base pair rather than four bases picks this. Each position on a strand can hold any of four bases, so the base is 4, not 2.
questions.explain: Each of the 10 positions can be any of four bases, independently of the others, so the number of possible sequences is 4 × 4 × … (10 times) = 4¹⁰ = 1 048 576.

questions.q: The human gene for insulin was inserted into a bacterium, which then produced insulin identical to the human protein. Which conclusion does this best support, and why?
options: Humans and bacteria share the same genes, because the bacterium already carried all the information needed to make human insulin.
The bacterium adopted the human genetic code in place of its own bacterial code when the human gene was inserted.
Any organism could translate any gene, because the code we observe is the only one that is chemically possible.
The genetic code is shared by humans and bacteria, because the bacterium translated human triplets into the same amino acids.
optionWhy: A student who takes a universal code to mean shared sequences picks this. Bacteria have no insulin gene; the gene had to be inserted, and only the code for reading it is shared.
A student who thinks each species has its own code picks this. There is no separate human code to adopt; the same code is used by both organisms, which is why the gene worked.
A student who assumes the codon assignments are fixed by chemistry picks this. The assignments are arbitrary, so sharing them is evidence of common ancestry, not chemical necessity.

The bacterium read the human gene's base triplets exactly as human cells do, producing the same amino acid sequence. This conservation of the genetic code across life forms is evidence of universal common ancestry.
questions.explain: The bacterium read the human gene's base triplets exactly as human cells do, producing the same amino acid sequence. This conservation of the genetic code across life forms is evidence of universal common ancestry.

questions.q: In a photomicrograph taken at a magnification of ×2000, a red blood cell measures 15 mm across. What is the actual width of the cell?
options: 7.5 µm
optionWhy: A student who multiplies the image size by the magnification picks this: 15 mm × 2000. That would make the real cell 30 m wide, larger than the image; actual size is image size divided by magnification.
Actual size = size of image ÷ magnification = 15 mm ÷ 2000 = 0.0075 mm, which is 7.5 µm (1 mm = 1000 µm), the typical diameter of a red blood cell.
A student who converts 0.0075 mm to micrometres using a factor of 100 picks this. 1 mm = 1000 µm, so 0.0075 mm = 7.5 µm; a cell 0.75 µm across would be smaller than most bacteria.
A student who converts 0.0075 mm to micrometres using a factor of 10 picks this. 0.075 µm is 75 nm, about the size of a large virus; 1 mm = 1000 µm, so 0.0075 mm = 7.5 µm.
questions.explain: Actual size = size of image ÷ magnification = 15 mm ÷ 2000 = 0.0075 mm, which is 7.5 µm (1 mm = 1000 µm), the typical diameter of a red blood cell.

questions.q: Ribosomes are about 25 nm across. They cannot be seen with a light microscope but are clearly visible in electron micrographs. What is the reason?
options: The electron microscope magnifies many more times, so much smaller objects become visible.
Electrons have a far shorter wavelength than light, so the resolution is much higher.
Heavy-metal stains used for electron microscopy make small structures much sharper.
Electron microscopes use fluorescent stains that make ribosomes glow in the dark.
optionWhy: A student who explains everything by magnification picks this. Magnifying a light microscope image further would only enlarge the blur; without higher resolution, objects closer together than 200 nm remain indistinguishable.

Resolution is limited by the wavelength of the radiation used. Light limits a light microscope to about 200 nm, so a 25 nm ribosome cannot be resolved; the electron beam's much shorter wavelength gives resolution below 1 nm.
A student who credits stains with sharpness picks this. Stains add contrast by scattering electrons; they cannot reveal detail finer than the resolution of the microscope, which is set by wavelength.

A student who lumps all advanced techniques together picks this. Fluorescent stains are used in light microscopy, and they do not raise its resolution; ribosomes are resolved by the short wavelength of electrons.
questions.explain: Resolution is limited by the wavelength of the radiation used. Light limits a light microscope to about 200 nm, so a 25 nm ribosome cannot be resolved; the electron beam's much shorter wavelength gives resolution below 1 nm.

questions.q: Which description of the structure of a Bacillus cell is correct?
options: The DNA is enclosed by a nuclear membrane inside a small nucleus within the cytoplasm.
The cell wall outside the plasma membrane is built from long parallel fibres of cellulose.
A loop of naked DNA lies in the cytoplasm, and proteins are made on 70S ribosomes.
The DNA loop is wound around histone proteins to package it within the nucleoid region.
optionWhy: A student who expects every cell to have a nucleus picks this. Prokaryotic DNA lies in the cytoplasm in a nucleoid region that is not enclosed by any membrane.
A student who assumes every cell wall is a cellulose wall picks this. The cell wall of Bacillus is made of peptidoglycan; cellulose walls are found only in plant cells.

A Gram-positive eubacterium such as Bacillus has a cell wall, a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, naked DNA in a loop lying in the nucleoid region of the cytoplasm, and 70S ribosomes on which its proteins are synthesized.
A student who thinks 'naked' refers only to the absence of a membrane picks this. Naked DNA is DNA not associated with histones; the prokaryotic loop has no histones.
questions.explain: A Gram-positive eubacterium such as Bacillus has a cell wall, a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, naked DNA in a loop lying in the nucleoid region of the cytoplasm, and 70S ribosomes on which its proteins are synthesized.

questions.q: Paramecium is a unicellular organism that lives in fresh water. Which statement correctly identifies one of its functions of life?
options: Growth: dividing by binary fission, so that the single cell becomes two separate cells.
Excretion: a process not carried out, because removing metabolic waste requires organs such as kidneys.
Homeostasis: expelling water that enters by osmosis, keeping the water content of the cytoplasm within limits.
Metabolism: releasing energy from food by respiration, without building up any new molecules.
optionWhy: A student who sees division as the organism getting bigger picks this. In a unicellular organism the cell is the organism, so division produces two organisms: that is reproduction. Growth is the increase in cell size between divisions.

A student who ties excretion to organs picks this. A single cell must carry out every function of life; the waste products of its metabolism, such as carbon dioxide, leave by diffusion across the plasma membrane.

Water enters continuously by osmosis; the contractile vacuole collects it and expels it, keeping the internal water content within limits. The water is not a product of metabolism, so this is homeostasis rather than excretion.

A student who uses the everyday meaning of metabolism picks this. Metabolism is all the enzyme-catalysed reactions of the cell, including the synthesis of proteins and other molecules as well as respiration.
questions.explain: Water enters continuously by osmosis; the contractile vacuole collects it and expels it, keeping the internal water content within limits. The water is not a product of metabolism, so this is homeostasis rather than excretion.

questions.q: Which row correctly compares the cells of animals, fungi and plants?
options: Cell wall: absent in animals, made of cellulose in fungi, made of cellulose in plants.
Vacuoles: absent in animals, present in fungi, present as a large sap vacuole in plants.
Centrioles: present in animals, absent in fungi, present in plants to form the spindle.
Cell wall: absent in animals, made of chitin in fungi, made of cellulose in plants.
optionWhy: A student who groups fungi with plants picks this. Fungal cell walls are made of chitin, not cellulose; only plant cells have cellulose walls.

A student who remembers 'vacuole: plants only' picks this. Animal cells have small temporary vacuoles; the difference from the large permanent sap vacuole of plant cells is in size and function, not presence.
A student who thinks a spindle needs centrioles picks this. Plant cells lack centrioles and organize their spindle without them; centrioles are a feature of animal cells.

Animal cells have no cell wall. Fungal cell walls are made of chitin and plant cell walls of cellulose; the presence and composition of the wall is one of the main differences between the three groups.
questions.explain: Animal cells have no cell wall. Fungal cell walls are made of chitin and plant cell walls of cellulose; the presence and composition of the wall is one of the main differences between the three groups.

questions.q: An electron micrograph shows a cell about 3 µm long. It has a cell wall, a paler fibrous region of DNA not enclosed by any membrane, many small dense granules, and no membrane-bound organelles. How should the cell be classified?
options: As a plant cell, because a cell wall is found only around the cells of plants.
As a eukaryote, because the region containing DNA must be a nucleus, as every cell has one.
As a prokaryote, because its DNA lies in a nucleoid region and it has no membrane-bound organelles.
As a eukaryote, because prokaryotic cells are too simple to contain any ribosomes.
optionWhy: A student who takes a cell wall to mean 'plant' picks this. Prokaryotes and fungi also have cell walls; a plant cell would show a nucleus, a sap vacuole and other membrane-bound organelles.

A student who believes every cell has a nucleus reads the nucleoid as a nucleus. A nucleus is bounded by a double membrane; DNA lying in the cytoplasm with no membrane is a nucleoid, a prokaryotic feature.

A nucleoid region of DNA without a membrane, the absence of membrane-bound organelles and the small size identify a prokaryote; the granules are 70S ribosomes and the cell wall is consistent with a bacterium.
A student who counts ribosomes as eukaryotic organelles picks this. All cells have ribosomes; the small dense granules are the 70S ribosomes of a prokaryote.
questions.explain: A nucleoid region of DNA without a membrane, the absence of membrane-bound organelles and the small size identify a prokaryote; the granules are 70S ribosomes and the cell wall is consistent with a bacterium.

questions.q: A student draws a cell from an electron micrograph of a gland that secretes enzymes, and must annotate each structure with its function. Which annotation is correct?
options: Rough endoplasmic reticulum — synthesizes proteins that are destined for secretion from the cell.
Golgi apparatus — synthesizes the enzymes that the cell will later secrete by exocytosis.
Microvilli — beat rhythmically to move the secreted enzymes along the surface of the cell.
Secretory vesicles — break down worn-out organelles inside the cell using the hydrolytic enzymes they hold.
optionWhy: Ribosomes attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum synthesize proteins for secretion, which pass into the reticulum and are carried in vesicles to the Golgi apparatus, then to the plasma membrane in secretory vesicles.
A student who gives the Golgi apparatus the job of protein synthesis picks this. Proteins are synthesized only on ribosomes; the Golgi apparatus modifies and packages them into vesicles.
A student who confuses microvilli with cilia picks this. Microvilli are static folds of the plasma membrane that increase surface area; they do not beat.

A student who treats all small vesicles as lysosomes picks this. Secretory vesicles carry the cell's products to the plasma membrane for release by exocytosis; digestion of organelles is the role of lysosomes.
questions.explain: Ribosomes attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum synthesize proteins for secretion, which pass into the reticulum and are carried in vesicles to the Golgi apparatus, then to the plasma membrane in secretory vesicles.
